scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance originated in the highland pastoral communities of Northern Greece, specifically Vlasti.
It served as a ritual reunion for sheep and cattle farmers before they moved to winter pastures.
Historically, it is tied to the August 15th festivities of the Dormition of the Virgin Mary.
on_screen: Map: Greece · Europe
Image — MISSING

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The primary occasion is the August 15th (Dekapentavgoustos) festival.
It signifies the reunion of the community, both historically for shepherds and currently for urban migrants returning to their ancestral village.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Dancers of all ages form a large open circle.
They hold hands and move in a slow, imposing rhythm.
The movement is synchronized with a cappella singing performed by the dancers themselves, rather than instrumental accompaniment.
Watch for The Grand Circle.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: In Vlasti, the dance is performed strictly a cappella.
There are no musical instruments; the dancers sing traditional songs to provide the rhythm and melody.
Listen for the None (a cappella).

The sound is defined entirely by the human voice. A large group of dancers sings in unison or harmony without any instrumental backing, creating a raw, resonant acoustic effect that fills the mountain air.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Individual figures are not highlighted in the sources; the dance is a collective communal expression involving 'dancers of all ages'.
A major variant exists in Syrrako, where the dance is accompanied by a band and singers, and serves as an opportunity to speak the Vlach language.
The dance is a subclass of Greek folk dance and is part of the broader tradition of ritualistic circle dances found in the Balkan highlands.
